learningObjectives.title: What a radical is and how to show one
Homolytic fission and the initiation step
Propagation, termination and the product mixture
Coordination bonds; nucleophiles are Lewis bases
Ligands and the charge on a complex ion
The leaving group and the rate
Carbocation stability and the major product

questions.q: Which species is a radical, and for what reason? Any charge on a species is shown, but unpaired electrons are not marked.
options: BF₃, because boron has only 6, not 8, outer-shell electrons
C₂H₅, because it has an odd number (13) of valence electrons
OH⁻, because it has one more electron than a neutral OH group
Cl₂, because it reacts vigorously with many substances
optionWhy: Boron does have only six outer electrons in BF₃, an incomplete octet, but that is not what makes a radical. BF₃ has 3 + 3 × 7 = 24 valence electrons, all paired, so it has no unpaired electron.
Count the valence electrons: 2 × 4 + 5 × 1 = 13. An odd number of electrons cannot all be paired, so one is unpaired: this is the ethyl radical, •C₂H₅ (usually written •CH₂CH₃).
A charge does not make a radical. OH⁻ has 6 + 1 + 1 = 8 valence electrons, all paired, so it is an ion but not a radical. It is the neutral OH species, with 7 valence electrons, that is a radical.

Chlorine is highly reactive, but reactivity is not the test for a radical. Cl₂ has 14 valence electrons, all paired (one bonding pair and six lone pairs). It forms radicals only when UV light or heat breaks the Cl–Cl bond.
questions.explain: Count the valence electrons: 2 × 4 + 5 × 1 = 13. An odd number of electrons cannot all be paired, so one is unpaired: this is the ethyl radical, •C₂H₅ (usually written •CH₂CH₃).

questions.q: Bromine reacts with methane in ultraviolet (UV) light. The diagram shows two drawings of the Br–Br bond in Br₂ breaking. Which statement about the drawings is correct?
options: Br₂ splits into Br⁺ and Br⁻ in the initiation step, as Drawing Q shows
Drawings P and Q show the same process, as each moves two electrons
In Drawing P, each arrow shows one bromine atom moving to a new position
Drawing P shows the initiation step, forming two Br• radicals
optionWhy: Drawing Q does show a bond splitting into ions: the double-barbed arrow moves BOTH bonding electrons to the right-hand Br, giving Br⁻ and Br⁺ (heterolytic fission). But that is not how Br₂ breaks in UV light. The initiation step is homolytic: the pair is shared out one electron to each atom, and no ions form.

The number of barbs matters. Drawing P moves one electron to each atom (two radicals); Drawing Q moves the pair to one atom (two ions). Two electrons leave the bond in both, but they end up in different places, so the products differ.

A student who reads mechanism arrows as atom movements picks this. Each arrow in Drawing P starts at the bond, where the bonding electrons are, and ends on the atom that receives one of them: the arrows track electrons, not atoms.

Each single-barbed arrow moves ONE electron of the Br–Br bonding pair to a different Br atom, so each atom leaves with one unpaired electron: Br₂ → 2Br•. This is homolytic fission, the initiation step of the chain reaction.
questions.explain: Each single-barbed arrow moves ONE electron of the Br–Br bonding pair to a different Br atom, so each atom leaves with one unpaired electron: Br₂ → 2Br•. This is homolytic fission, the initiation step of the chain reaction.

questions.q: A student claims: 'Chlorine radicals are used up in the propagation steps, so every molecule of CH₃Cl formed from methane and chlorine needs a new Cl• from the initiation step.' Which evaluation of this claim is correct?
options: Incorrect: the H• formed in the first step reacts with Cl₂ to re-form Cl• for the chain
Correct: each propagation step uses up a radical, so each CH₃Cl needs a new initiation
Correct: CH₃Cl forms when •CH₃ and Cl• combine, which uses up two radicals each time
Incorrect: the Cl• used in the first step is re-formed in the second, so it can react again
optionWhy: The claim is wrong, but not for this reason. No H• forms: the first propagation step is CH₄ + Cl• → •CH₃ + HCl. The Cl• is regenerated when •CH₃ reacts with Cl₂.
Count the radicals on each side of a propagation step: one on the left and one on the right. Propagation does not change the number of radicals; only termination removes them.
That termination step does occur, but it is rare because radicals are present at very low concentration. Most CH₃Cl forms in propagation, •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•, which regenerates Cl•.

In CH₄ + Cl• → •CH₃ + HCl a Cl• is used, and in •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl• a Cl• is formed. Each cycle regenerates the radical, so one initiation event can lead to many CH₃Cl molecules: a chain reaction.
questions.explain: In CH₄ + Cl• → •CH₃ + HCl a Cl• is used, and in •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl• a Cl• is formed. Each cycle regenerates the radical, so one initiation event can lead to many CH₃Cl molecules: a chain reaction.

questions.q: The diagram shows the electron movements in a propagation step of the reaction of methane with chlorine. Which products does the step shown form?
options: CH₃Cl and a chloride ion
CH₃Cl and a Cl• radical
CH₃Cl and an HCl molecule
CH₃Cl alone, with no radical
optionWhy: Arrow 3 is single-barbed, so it moves only ONE electron to the far Cl. That atom keeps one electron of the broken bond and is neutral with an unpaired electron, Cl•. A Cl⁻ ion would need a double-barbed arrow bringing the whole pair, and no ion forms in this radical step.

Arrows 1 and 2 each bring ONE electron into the space between C and the nearer Cl, forming the C–Cl bond of CH₃Cl. Arrow 3 moves the other electron of the Cl–Cl bond to the far Cl, which leaves with one unpaired electron: •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•. The Cl• formed carries the chain on.

CH₃Cl and HCl are the products of the OVERALL equation, not of this step. No hydrogen atom takes part in the drawing: the arrows show only the C–Cl bond forming and the Cl–Cl bond breaking. HCl is made in the other propagation step, CH₄ + Cl• → •CH₃ + HCl.

A student who thinks radicals are used up in propagation picks this. Count the atoms: Cl₂ brings two Cl atoms. Arrow 2 puts one bonding electron into the new C–Cl bond and arrow 3 sends the other to the far Cl, which leaves as Cl•. Each propagation step regenerates a radical, which is why one initiation event makes many CH₃Cl molecules.
questions.explain: Arrows 1 and 2 each bring ONE electron into the space between C and the nearer Cl, forming the C–Cl bond of CH₃Cl. Arrow 3 moves the other electron of the Cl–Cl bond to the far Cl, which leaves with one unpaired electron: •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•. The Cl• formed carries the chain on.

questions.q:
2-bromo-2-methylpropane reacts with water:
(CH₃)₃CBr + H₂O → (CH₃)₃COH + HBr
Which reactant acts as the nucleophile, and why?
options: Neither, as neither reactant carries a negative charge
(CH₃)₃CBr, as its C atom accepts a pair of electrons
H₂O, as its O atom and the C atom each give one electron
H₂O, as a lone pair on its O atom forms the new bond to carbon
optionWhy: A nucleophile needs an electron pair to donate, not a negative charge. Both reactants are neutral, but a lone pair on the O atom of H₂O forms the new C–O bond, so water is the nucleophile.
Accepting an electron pair is the role of the electrophile. The carbon of (CH₃)₃CBr is the electron-deficient site that is attacked; the donor, H₂O, is the nucleophile.
H₂O is the nucleophile, but not for this reason. The new C–O bond is made from a lone pair on oxygen; the carbon supplies no electrons.
The O atom of water has lone pairs; one is donated to the electron-deficient carbon atom, forming the C–O bond of the alcohol. A neutral molecule can be a nucleophile.
questions.explain: The O atom of water has lone pairs; one is donated to the electron-deficient carbon atom, forming the C–O bond of the alcohol. A neutral molecule can be a nucleophile.

questions.q: In the reaction CH₃CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂OH + Br⁻ a new C–O bond forms. Where do the two electrons of the new C–O bond come from?
options: One from the O atom and one from the C atom
Both from the C–Br bond, which becomes the new C–O bond
Both from a lone pair on the O atom of the OH⁻ ion
Both from the C atom, which donates them to the O
optionWhy: Dot-and-cross diagrams show each atom giving one electron, but here the nucleophile supplies both. The carbon's electrons in the C–Br bond leave with Br⁻.
The C–Br pair is not handed over to O: it moves onto Br, which leaves as Br⁻ carrying both electrons. The new C–O pair is a lone pair donated by the O of OH⁻.
OH⁻ is the nucleophile: a lone pair on its oxygen is donated to the δ+ carbon and becomes the C–O bonding pair. The C–Br pair leaves with Br⁻.
This makes the halogenoalkane carbon the donor. The carbon is δ+ and electron-deficient, so it accepts the pair; the electron-rich OH⁻ donates it.
questions.explain: OH⁻ is the nucleophile: a lone pair on its oxygen is donated to the δ+ carbon and becomes the C–O bonding pair. The C–Br pair leaves with Br⁻.

questions.q: Water can undergo heterolytic fission of one O–H bond to form H⁺ and OH⁻. The diagram shows four attempts, P to S, to draw this change with a curly arrow. Which drawing is correct?
options: Drawing Q
Drawing P
Drawing R
Drawing S
optionWhy: This arrow sends the bonding pair to H, which would form H⁻ and OH⁺. Gaining the pair makes a fragment negative, not positive, so to form OH⁻ the pair must go to the OH group.
A curly arrow starts where the electron pair is (the H–OH bond) and ends where it goes. Both bonding electrons go to oxygen, so OH takes the pair and becomes OH⁻, leaving H with no electrons: H⁺.

Each fish-hook arrow moves ONE electron, so R shows homolytic fission: one electron to each fragment, giving the radicals H• and •OH, not ions. To form H⁺ and OH⁻ both electrons must go to OH, shown by a single double-barbed arrow from the bond to OH.
A curly arrow is drawn from the electrons, not from the atom that receives them. It starts at the H–OH bonding pair and ends on the OH group; it is not drawn from OH back toward the bond.
questions.explain: A curly arrow starts where the electron pair is (the H–OH bond) and ends where it goes. Both bonding electrons go to oxygen, so OH takes the pair and becomes OH⁻, leaving H with no electrons: H⁺.

questions.q:
Ammonia reacts with hydrogen ions:
NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺
Which species acts as the electrophile?
options: NH₃, as its nitrogen atom carries a lone pair of electrons
Neither, as N and H each supply one electron to the bond
H⁺, as it accepts the lone pair on the nitrogen atom
H⁺, as it forms an ionic bond with the nitrogen atom of NH₃
optionWhy: Having a lone pair to donate makes NH₃ the nucleophile (the electron-pair donor). The electrophile is the acceptor, H⁺.
H⁺ has no electrons, so it cannot supply one. Both electrons of the new N–H bond come from the nitrogen lone pair; H⁺ accepts them and is the electrophile.
H⁺ has no electrons and accepts the lone pair of nitrogen to form the new N–H bond. A positively charged species that accepts a pair is an electrophile.
H⁺ is the electrophile, but the bond it forms is covalent: the nitrogen lone pair is shared between N and H. NH₄⁺ has four identical covalent N–H bonds.
questions.explain: H⁺ has no electrons and accepts the lone pair of nitrogen to form the new N–H bond. A positively charged species that accepts a pair is an electrophile.

questions.q: But-2-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₃, undergoes hydration when heated with steam in the presence of an acid catalyst. Which statement is correct?
options: Water adds across the C=C bond, forming butane-2,3-diol.
An OH group replaces an H atom, forming but-2-en-2-ol.
H atoms from water add across C=C, forming butane.
Water adds across the C=C bond, forming butan-2-ol.
optionWhy: A diol would need an OH group on both carbons, but water supplies only one OH. One carbon receives H and the other OH, giving butan-2-ol.
Alkenes react by addition, not substitution. The C=C bond becomes a single bond as H and OH add across it, giving butan-2-ol.
Adding hydrogen to form an alkane is hydrogenation (H₂ with a catalyst). Hydration adds both parts of water, H and OH, giving butan-2-ol.
H adds to one carbon of C=C and OH to the other: CH₃CH=CHCH₃ + H₂O → CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃, butan-2-ol.
questions.explain: H adds to one carbon of C=C and OH to the other: CH₃CH=CHCH₃ + H₂O → CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃, butan-2-ol.

questions.q: Ethene is mixed with hydrogen bromide gas at room temperature. Which statement is correct?
options: HBr adds across the C=C bond, forming CH₂BrCH₂Br.
A Br atom replaces one H atom, forming CH₂=CHBr.
HBr adds across the C=C bond, forming CH₃CH₂Br.
No reaction occurs, as the HBr molecule is neutral.
optionWhy: HBr has only one Br atom, so it cannot put Br on both carbons. One carbon gains H and the other gains Br, giving CH₃CH₂Br.
Substitution that keeps C=C is not how alkenes react. HBr adds across the double bond, giving CH₃CH₂Br with no C=C bond.
H adds to one carbon and Br to the other: CH₂=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CH₂Br, bromoethane.
A neutral molecule can be an electrophile. HBr accepts an electron pair from the C=C bond at its δ+ H atom, and bromoethane forms.
questions.explain: H adds to one carbon and Br to the other: CH₂=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CH₂Br, bromoethane.

questions.q: In the first step of the acid-catalysed addition of water to ethene, H⁺ bonds to one carbon atom of the C=C bond, forming CH₃CH₂⁺. Which species acts as the Lewis base in this step?
options: Neither, as ethene has no lone pair to donate
H⁺, as it accepts the electron pair of the C=C bond
Ethene, as its C=C electrons form the new C–H bond
Ethene, as it gives two electrons to H⁺ in an ionic bond
optionWhy: A Lewis base needs an available electron pair, not necessarily a lone pair. The electron pair of the C=C second bond is donated to H⁺.
Accepting an electron pair makes H⁺ the Lewis ACID. The Lewis base is the donor, ethene.
The electron pair of the second bond of C=C is donated to H⁺ and becomes the new C–H bond. The electron-pair donor, ethene, is the Lewis base; H⁺ is the Lewis acid.
Ethene is the Lewis base, but the bond formed is covalent: the donated pair is shared between C and H in the new C–H bond.
questions.explain: The electron pair of the second bond of C=C is donated to H⁺ and becomes the new C–H bond. The electron-pair donor, ethene, is the Lewis base; H⁺ is the Lewis acid.

questions.q: Ammonia reacts with boron trifluoride to form H₃NBF₃. The Lewis formula of the product is often drawn with a positive formal charge on N and a negative formal charge on B. Which statement about the new N–B bond is correct?
options: It is a coordination bond; both electrons came from N
It is a coordination bond; both of its electrons came from B
It is a covalent bond; N and B each gave an electron
It is an ionic bond, as N carries + and B carries −
optionWhy: N in NH₃ has a lone pair and B in BF₃ has only six outer electrons. N donates its lone pair to B, forming a coordination bond; the formal charges record this donation.
BF₃ is the Lewis acid, the acceptor. B has no lone pair to donate; the pair comes from the nitrogen of NH₃, the Lewis base.
Each atom giving one electron is the dot-and-cross picture of an ordinary covalent bond. Here both electrons come from the N lone pair, so it is a coordination bond.
The + and − are formal charges in one molecule, not the charges of separate ions. N and B share the donated pair, so the bond is covalent (coordination).
questions.explain: N in NH₃ has a lone pair and B in BF₃ has only six outer electrons. N donates its lone pair to B, forming a coordination bond; the formal charges record this donation.

questions.q: The diagram shows the reactants in the reaction BF₃ + F⁻ → BF₄⁻, with a curly arrow. BF₃ is drawn as a displayed formula; all four lone pairs of F⁻ are shown. Which statement about the reaction is correct?
options: F⁻ is the Lewis acid, since it is the species that donates the electron pair
Neither species is an acid or a base, since no H⁺ ion is transferred
B and F each supply one electron to the new bond, as in the other three B–F bonds
F⁻ is the Lewis base, since it supplies both electrons of the coordination bond
optionWhy: A Lewis acid ACCEPTS an electron pair. F⁻ donates the pair shown by the arrow, so it is the Lewis base; BF₃, whose B atom accepts the pair, is the Lewis acid.
Lewis theory does not require hydrogen. Any electron-pair donor is a Lewis base and any acceptor a Lewis acid, so BF₃ (acceptor) and F⁻ (donor) are a Lewis acid–base pair.

The arrow starts at a lone pair on F⁻, so both electrons of the new bond come from F⁻; B contributes none. Once formed, this coordination bond is the same as the other B–F bonds, but its electrons came from one atom.

The arrow starts at a lone pair on F⁻ and ends on B, which has only six electrons and an empty orbital. F⁻ donates the pair (Lewis base), BF₃ accepts it (Lewis acid), and a bond in which both electrons come from one atom is a coordination bond.
questions.explain: The arrow starts at a lone pair on F⁻ and ends on B, which has only six electrons and an empty orbital. F⁻ donates the pair (Lewis base), BF₃ accepts it (Lewis acid), and a bond in which both electrons come from one atom is a coordination bond.

questions.q: The diagram shows a complex ion of cobalt with its ligands, drawn inside square brackets with the overall charge of the ion outside. What is the charge on the cobalt ion in this complex?
optionWhy: This takes the overall charge outside the brackets as the charge on the metal. The two Cl⁻ ligands contribute −2, so the cobalt ion must be +3 for the complex to be +1.
Count the ligand charges from the diagram: four neutral NH₃ and two Cl⁻ give −2 in total. For the overall charge to be +1 the metal must be +3: (+3) + 2(−1) + 4(0) = +1.
This counts all six ligands as −1: +1 + 6 = +7. Donating a lone pair does not give a ligand a charge; NH₃ is neutral, and only the two Cl⁻ ligands carry −1, so the metal is +3.
This adds the size of the Cl⁻ charges to the metal charge, x + 2 = +1, giving x = −1. Charges are combined with their signs: x + 2(−1) = +1, so x = +3.
questions.explain: Count the ligand charges from the diagram: four neutral NH₃ and two Cl⁻ give −2 in total. For the overall charge to be +1 the metal must be +3: (+3) + 2(−1) + 4(0) = +1.
questions.working: Overall charge = charge on metal ion + sum of ligand charges. The diagram shows four NH₃ ligands (each 0), two Cl⁻ ligands (each −1) and an overall charge of +1: +1 = x + 4(0) + 2(−1), so x = +1 + 2 = +3. The ion is [CoCl₂(NH₃)₄]⁺ containing Co³⁺.

questions.q: A primary halogenoalkane and a tertiary halogenoalkane each react with aqueous hydroxide ions. The diagram shows the energy profiles, P and Q, of the two reactions. Which statement is correct?
options: Q is for the tertiary halogenoalkane, as its dip is the carbocation intermediate
P is for the tertiary halogenoalkane, as its single peak shows a one-step mechanism
Q is for the primary halogenoalkane, as its carbocation is the more stable one
P is for the primary halogenoalkane, as its peak is the intermediate of the reaction
optionWhy: Two peaks mean two steps with an intermediate between them. A tertiary halogenoalkane reacts by SN1: slow heterolysis of C–X gives a carbocation (the dip, high in energy but a real species), then OH⁻ attacks it. The one-peak profile P is the concerted SN2 reaction of a primary halogenoalkane.

A tertiary halogenoalkane reacts by SN1, and the '1' means one species in the rate-determining step, not one step. SN1 has two steps and so two peaks (profile Q); the single peak of P is the concerted SN2 reaction of the primary halogenoalkane.

Alkyl groups release electron density, so a primary carbocation is the LEAST stable and does not form. Primary halogenoalkanes react in one concerted step (profile P); tertiary ones form a tertiary carbocation (profile Q).

P is indeed the one-step SN2 profile of the primary halogenoalkane, but its peak is a transition state, not an intermediate. The species at the top has partial bonds to both OH and the halogen, exists only momentarily and cannot be isolated. An intermediate sits in a dip between two peaks, like the carbocation in Q.
questions.explain: Two peaks mean two steps with an intermediate between them. A tertiary halogenoalkane reacts by SN1: slow heterolysis of C–X gives a carbocation (the dip, high in energy but a real species), then OH⁻ attacks it. The one-peak profile P is the concerted SN2 reaction of a primary halogenoalkane.

questions.q: Under identical conditions, which reacts faster with aqueous hydroxide ions, 1-bromobutane or 1-chlorobutane, and why?
options: 1-chlorobutane, as the C–Cl bond is more polar than C–Br
1-chlorobutane, as the smaller Cl atom blocks attack less
Neither; both react at the same rate, as OH⁻ attacks C
1-bromobutane, as the C–Br bond is weaker than the C–Cl bond
optionWhy: C–Cl is more polar, but the rate is controlled by how easily the C–X bond breaks. C–Cl is stronger, so 1-chlorobutane reacts more slowly.
The nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the halogen, so the halogen's size does not block it. The weaker C–Br bond makes 1-bromobutane faster.
OH⁻ does attack carbon, but the C–X bond must also break, and its strength depends on the halogen. C–Br is weaker than C–Cl, so 1-bromobutane reacts faster.
The C–Br bond enthalpy is lower than that of C–Cl, so it breaks more easily and bromide is the better leaving group. 1-bromobutane reacts faster.
questions.explain: The C–Br bond enthalpy is lower than that of C–Cl, so it breaks more easily and bromide is the better leaving group. 1-bromobutane reacts faster.

questions.q: In the acid-catalysed addition of water to ethene, the first step forms the carbocation CH₃CH₂⁺. Which describes what happens next?
options: A lone pair on the O of H₂O bonds to C⁺, then H⁺ is lost, regenerating the catalyst.
A lone pair on the O of H₂O bonds to C⁺, and the H⁺ stays, so the acid is used up.
The C⁺ ion donates an electron pair to the O atom of H₂O, forming a C–O bond.
H₂O first ionizes to OH⁻, as only a negative ion can bond to the C⁺ ion.
optionWhy: Water is the nucleophile: an O lone pair forms the C–O bond, giving CH₃CH₂OH₂⁺. This loses H⁺ (curly arrow from the O–H bond to O), giving ethanol and regenerating the H⁺ catalyst.
The first part is right, but the catalyst is not consumed. CH₃CH₂OH₂⁺ loses H⁺ to give ethanol, so the H⁺ used in the first step is regenerated.
The carbocation has an empty orbital and no pair to donate; it is the electrophile. The O atom of H₂O donates a lone pair to the positive carbon.
A neutral molecule with a lone pair can be a nucleophile. In the acidic mixture H₂O itself bonds to C⁺; OH⁻ is not needed.
questions.explain: Water is the nucleophile: an O lone pair forms the C–O bond, giving CH₃CH₂OH₂⁺. This loses H⁺ (curly arrow from the O–H bond to O), giving ethanol and regenerating the H⁺ catalyst.

questions.q: But-1-ene, CH₃CH₂CH=CH₂, reacts with hydrogen bromide. The diagram shows skeletal formulas of the two carbocations, P and Q, that could form when H⁺ adds to the C=C bond. Which statement is correct?
options: Q forms faster, as its positive carbon has only one electron-withdrawing alkyl group
Q forms, as the H atom adds to the carbon atom of C=C that has fewer H atoms
P forms faster, as its positive carbon is stabilized by two electron-releasing alkyl groups
P and Q form in equal amounts, since H⁺ can add to either carbon of C=C
optionWhy: Alkyl groups release electron density to a positive carbon; they do not withdraw it. More alkyl groups mean a more stable carbocation, so the secondary carbocation P is favoured over the primary Q.
The rule runs the other way: H adds to the carbon with MORE hydrogen atoms (the CH₂ end), so that the positive charge sits on the more substituted carbon. That gives P, the secondary carbocation.

In P the + is on a carbon bonded to two other carbons (a secondary carbocation, CH₃CH₂CH⁺CH₃); in Q it is on an end carbon bonded to one (primary). Alkyl groups release electron density towards the positive carbon, so P is more stable, forms faster, and gives the major product 2-bromobutane.
The two directions of addition give carbocations of different stability. The secondary carbocation P has a much lower activation energy, so it forms far faster and 2-bromobutane is the major product.
questions.explain: In P the + is on a carbon bonded to two other carbons (a secondary carbocation, CH₃CH₂CH⁺CH₃); in Q it is on an end carbon bonded to one (primary). Alkyl groups release electron density towards the positive carbon, so P is more stable, forms faster, and gives the major product 2-bromobutane.

questions.q: Benzene reacts with a charged electrophile, E⁺. Which sequence describes the mechanism?
options: Ring π electrons bond to E⁺, forming a cation; loss of H⁺ restores the ring.
Ring π electrons bond to E⁺, forming a cation; a nucleophile then adds to it.
E⁺ donates an electron pair to the ring, forming an anion; H⁻ is then lost.
E⁺ swaps directly with an H atom in one step; the ring stays delocalized.
optionWhy: A curly arrow from the delocalized ring to E⁺ forms the C–E bond and a positive intermediate. A curly arrow from the C–H bond into the ring then releases H⁺ and restores delocalization: C₆H₆ + E⁺ → C₆H₅E + H⁺.
Adding a nucleophile completes an alkene-style addition and would leave the ring non-aromatic. Benzene's intermediate loses H⁺ instead, restoring the stable ring.
E⁺ is the electrophile, so it accepts an electron pair from the ring. The intermediate is a cation, and it loses H⁺, not H⁻.
Substitution is not a one-step swap. E⁺ first bonds to the ring, forming a cation in which delocalization is partly broken; H⁺ is then lost.
questions.explain: A curly arrow from the delocalized ring to E⁺ forms the C–E bond and a positive intermediate. A curly arrow from the C–H bond into the ring then releases H⁺ and restores delocalization: C₆H₆ + E⁺ → C₆H₅E + H⁺.

questions.q: The diagram shows the intermediate formed when benzene reacts with an electrophile, E⁺, together with the curly arrow for the step that follows. What happens in the step shown?
options: A nucleophile adds to the positive carbon, giving an addition product
The C–H bonding pair moves into the ring, restoring delocalization, and H⁺ is lost
The C–H bond breaks homolytically, releasing a hydrogen atom, H•
The arrow shows the hydrogen atom moving to another carbon atom of the ring
optionWhy: Benzene does not react like an alkene here. Adding a nucleophile would leave the ring permanently non-aromatic; instead the C–H pair returns to the ring, H⁺ is lost, and the stable delocalized ring is regained (substitution).

The arrow starts at the C–H bond and ends in the ring. Both electrons of that bond re-enter the π system, so the six-carbon delocalization is restored, the ring loses its positive charge, and the hydrogen leaves without its electrons as H⁺: C₆H₆ + E⁺ → C₆H₅E + H⁺.
The arrow is a double-barbed curly arrow, so it moves a PAIR of electrons: heterolytic fission. Both electrons of the C–H bond go into the ring and the hydrogen leaves as H⁺, not as a radical.
Curly arrows show electrons, not atoms, moving. This arrow moves the C–H bonding pair into the ring; the hydrogen does not move around the ring, it is lost as H⁺.
questions.explain: The arrow starts at the C–H bond and ends in the ring. Both electrons of that bond re-enter the π system, so the six-carbon delocalization is restored, the ring loses its positive charge, and the hydrogen leaves without its electrons as H⁺: C₆H₆ + E⁺ → C₆H₅E + H⁺.
